# Research sources for Gilgit-Baltistan population change

Checked 27 October 2026. Study period: 1951–2025. This catalogue distinguishes sources whose relevant content was inspected from discovery leads, failed downloads and sources requiring further review. It is not a guarantee that every link remains available. The five PDFs supplied in chat provide the core evidence; external catalogue links do not establish byte-for-byte identity with those local files.

## Core supplied documents

| ID | Document | Why it matters | Locations reviewed closely |
|---|---|---|---|
| Y | *Gilgit-Baltistan Statistical Year Book 2024* | Historical and district census summaries, source conflicts, administrative context | Tables 3.2–3.14, PDF pp. 81–86 / printed pp. 59–64; introduction and selected adjacent tables. |
| I | *Unlocking Investment Opportunities in Gilgit Baltistan, Pakistan* (2024) | Economic context, the 2022 population estimate, hypotheses about seasonal movement and services | PDF pp. 20, 59–60, 74 and selected sector sections. It is a prospectus, not an independent census. |
| M16 | *Gilgit-Baltistan MICS 2016–17 Key Findings Report* | Earlier fertility, mortality, household and education indicators | Image-only PDF; relevant pages inspected visually, especially PDF pp. 7–8, 16–18, 20–21. |
| M24K | *MICS 2024–25 Key Findings Report* (December 2025) | Concise summary that must be checked against detailed tables | Text indexed; demographic summary and conflicting values visually checked. |
| M24F | *MICS 2024–25 Survey Findings Report* (December 2025) | Detailed survey design, estimates, denominators and sampling errors | Text indexed, with focused review of sampling, demographic, fertility, mortality and education sections; not individually read across all 731 pages. |

## Academic literature to build the explanatory review

| Reading | Contribution to this project | How far the evidence can be taken |
|---|---|---|
| Kreutzmann (1991), [The Karakoram Highway: The impact of road construction on mountain societies](https://lib.icimod.org/records/fmqwy-7m305), DOI [10.1017/S0026749X00010817](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0026749X00010817) | Historical framework for accessibility, transport and mountain–lowland integration. | Contextual mechanisms, not an estimated causal effect on total GB population. Repository metadata has a volume typo; verify against the paper when formatting a final bibliography. |
| Kreutzmann (1996), [settlement development in central Hunza](https://doi.org/10.3112/erdkunde.1996.03.02) | Settlement history, water infrastructure and migrant enclaves. | Original journal material available; local settlement evidence should not be generalized into a region-wide migration rate. |
| Kreutzmann (2001), [Societal developments in high mountain regions of South Asia exemplified by geolinguistic diversity](https://www.persee.fr/doc/rga_0035-1121_2001_num_89_2_4640?pageId=T1_149) | Links settlement, administrative functions and population movement. | Useful historical interpretation; distinguish towns from districts and the whole region. |
| Kreutzmann (2006), [People and Mountains](https://doi.org/10.57466/ger.10.1_49) | Rationale for mountain-specific disaggregation and careful use of national statistics. | Methodological context, not a current population source. Platform availability dates should not replace the paper’s publication year. |
| Ali et al. (2021 online / 2022 volume), [Factors shaping economics of land use change in Gilgit Baltistan, Pakistan](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10708-021-10478-3) | Mixed-method study of selected Ghizer, Hunza and Nagar sites; potential land-use extension. | Full text inspected. Selected sites and retrospective reporting limit regional generalization. Consult the linked correction before extracting detailed tables. |
| Shah et al. (2025), [Assessing urbanization and climate change impacts on environmental sustainability in Gilgit city](https://doi.org/10.1007/s44327-025-00113-y) | Land-cover analysis and interviews; example for a bounded city-scale extension. | Full text accessible. A conceptual DPSIR framework is not causal identification. |
| Sökefeld (2014 issue), [Disaster and (im)mobility: Restoring mobility in Gojal after the Attabad landslide](https://doi.org/10.15460/ethnoscripts.2014.16.1.785) | Qualitative account of disruption and mobility after a disaster. | Original landing page inspected. Current page metadata shows 2025, while issue/DOI identify 2014; preserve the discrepancy. Not a migration-rate estimate. |
| Ullah et al. (2024), [Socio-economic determinants of internal migration in Gilgit Baltistan](https://ijciss.org/index.php/ijciss/article/view/922) | Housing and infrastructure hypotheses from a small household study. | Original abstract describes 76 households; observational findings do not establish regional causality or prevalence. |
| [Constraints and prospects of utilising mountain pastures in Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13570-022-00253-5), Pastoralism (2022) | Livelihood change, roads, education/work movement and pastoral labour. | Relevant contextual study; not a human population benchmark. |
| [Migration and Translocal Development in the Karakoram and Himalayas](https://www.uni-augsburg.de/en/fakultaet/fai/geo/prof/geohum/transformationen-im-globalen-sueden/migration-und-translokale-entwicklung-karakorum-himalaya/), University of Augsburg | Research programme on education migration and multi-local livelihoods, including Gojal. | Project description, not a substitute for a completed study’s empirical results. |
| Butz (2011), [Accessibility interrupted: the Shimshal road, Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1541-0064.2011.00365.x) | Connectivity can be interrupted; helps avoid a simple progress narrative about roads. | Further reading lead; do not imply full-text appraisal was completed here. |
| [Drivers of Change to Mountain Sustainability in the Hindu Kush Himalaya](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-92288-1_2), assessment chapter (2019) | Wider regional context for migration and urbanization. | Synthesis context; keep local evidence separate from HKH-wide generalizations. |

## Priorities before publishing definitive results

Retrieve original historical enumeration tables and their geographic definitions; resolve the 1951 and 2017 source versions; obtain a dated district-boundary crosswalk; clarify the yearbook projection header and MICS summary/full-report differences; and confirm any microdata access directly through official channels. The 2025 observed population cell should stay empty until supported. No contact messages were sent and no restricted microdata were acquired during this research.

Website scraping should preserve provenance and access status rather than treat every retrieved number as equally reliable. Prefer direct official downloads and documented interfaces; retain source text and page images for audit, record failures, and avoid bypassing access controls. No independent gridded-population product was sufficiently verified here to recommend it as a validation dataset.


## Website research extension · 28 October 2026

### UNDP Pakistan — GLOF-II project

[Climate risk reaches households through land, water and roads](https://www.undp.org/pakistan/projects/scaling-glacial-lake-outburst-floods-risk-reduction-northern-pakistan-glof-ii-project)

UNDP identifies glacial-lake outburst floods as risks to homes and livelihoods in northern Pakistan. Damage to irrigation, farms and transport can disrupt income, schooling and access to services. These are plausible pressures on where households live; this source does not quantify the share of GB population change caused by climate change.

Evidence: Official programme evidence; mechanism, not migration attribution. Scope: GB and KP; regional programme totals are not GB-only.

### European Commission — Strengthening communities facing climate-related displacement

[Displacement requires durable services](https://international-partnerships.ec.europa.eu/policies/programming/projects/strengthening-communities-facing-climate-related-displacement-pakistan_en)

An EU-supported project specifically addresses displacement-affected communities in Gilgit-Baltistan through preparedness, infrastructure and integrated services. It identifies gaps in durable settlement planning. A project description establishes a documented policy concern, not a measured GB-wide displacement rate.

Evidence: Official project description; no GB-wide population estimate. Scope: Displacement-affected communities in GB.

### Farinotti et al. (2020) — Manifestations and mechanisms of the Karakoram glacier Anomaly

[Glacier change varies across the mountains](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6949123/)

A 2020 scientific review documented balanced or slightly positive glacier mass budgets in parts of the Karakoram during the preceding decades, alongside glacier surges. This historical variation means a single claim that every GB glacier is retreating is too simple. The review does not establish the condition of every glacier in 2025.

Evidence: Peer-reviewed synthesis; historical regional evidence. Scope: Karakoram, not all GB glaciers individually.

### Benz (2014) — Mobility, multilocality and translocal development

[Education and work connect mountain households to cities](https://gh.copernicus.org/articles/69/259/2014/)

Research on Karakoram livelihoods describes education, professional employment and income earned away from agriculture as parts of households’ strategies. Family members can live in several places and remain economically connected. Moving away therefore does not always mean permanent separation from a home village.

Evidence: Peer-reviewed local livelihood research; no current regional rate. Scope: Karakoram case-study evidence.

### Benz (2016) — Framing Modernization Interventions

[Documented destinations, without invented flows](https://d-nb.info/1162840749/34)

A study based on 2011–2012 fieldwork in Gojal describes educational connections to Karachi, Gilgit, Islamabad/Rawalpindi, Lahore and Peshawar, and some international family-linked moves. These examples document pathways; they are not a current destination ranking or the percentage of GB youth leaving.

Evidence: Peer-reviewed local fieldwork; historical destination examples. Scope: Hussaini and Passu / Gojal; not representative of all GB.

### Benz (2018) — Mobility (in)justice, positionality and translocal development in Gojal

[Who can move matters as much as who wants to](https://opus.bibliothek.uni-augsburg.de/opus4/files/66775/66775.pdf)

Research in Hussaini and Passu shows that kinship support, gender norms and position within a household shape access to education and jobs elsewhere. Mobility can improve opportunities while widening inequalities between people with different resources. A preference to migrate should not be confused with the ability to do so.

Evidence: Academic book chapter using local fieldwork; interpretive evidence. Scope: Two Gojal villages; 2011–2012 research.

### Shah et al. (2025) — Urbanization, climate change and environmental sustainability in Gilgit

[A city comparison needs services and exposure](https://doi.org/10.1007/s44327-025-00113-y)

A 2025 study of Gilgit combines land-cover analysis with expert interviews and discusses pressure on resources and hazard exposure as the city expands. A useful comparison of living conditions should examine education, health, housing, water, employment and disaster risk separately; this study does not support a single universal best-place ranking.

Evidence: Peer-reviewed city case study; mixed-method evidence. Scope: Gilgit city, not whole district or GB.

### Ali et al. (2021 online / 2022 volume) — Factors shaping economics of land use change

[Built-up growth is not a population counter](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10708-021-10478-3)

Research in selected urbanizing sites in Ghizer, Hunza and Nagar documents land-use and land-price changes using 2009, 2014 and 2019 reference years. It supports studying housing and agricultural-land pressure alongside demography. Built-up expansion alone cannot reveal how many residents moved in or why.

Evidence: Peer-reviewed mixed-method local study; observational evidence. Scope: Selected sites in Ghizer, Hunza and Nagar.

### Literacy and living conditions

Literacy uses 2017 Census figures reproduced in GB Yearbook table 3.9, PDF page 85 / printed 63. Internet, basic water and sanitation use MICS 2024–25 tables LN.6.1, WS.1.2 and WS.3.7 respectively. Exact denominators, values and provenance are supplied in living-data.json. No current district literacy series or matched overseas living-cost comparison was validated.
